items.content:
New talk on the open model economy. I wanted to break down the case of where open model builders should steer the economics of the industry, if we want to avoid being swallowed by OpenAI and Anthropic in due time. This rests fully on being able to drive the cost of inference down dramatically on specialized, repetitive tasks, rather than trying to compete on cost with the frontier labs in any general agent.

A core piece of it is how the open model economy is very fragmented, leaving an interesting puzzle we need to solve to get revenue from applications to feed back into the next model cycle. This is a very near-term problem as closed labs scale rapidly.

This talk investigates:
Are people using open models?
How close are open models to the frontier?
Mapping the open model economy
How open models win

This is a practice recording of my talk "How Open Models Win" for Fireworks Forge 2026 in San Francisco (3 November 2026), which will have improvements over this one.

We are collaborating with Silicon Data to bring market-based GPU pricing into AA-AgentPerf, our datacenter system performance benchmark

Our users and partners want to know how much agent work they can support per dollar of compute. @silicondata's rental price indices allow us to report a reliable value-for-money metric, updated daily as prices change. The new metric is Throughput per $/hr, which divides the total throughput of a system and serving configuration by the hourly cost of renting that system. Among systems with available rental pricing, NVIDIA’s B300 generally leads, while B200 matches it at faster output speeds on some models

items.content:
I decompiled probably my favorite game ever: Battlefield 1942 and I put it on the web with multiplayer for you to play here:

👉 https://t.co/6C8H8KtSaU 👈

(It's the free shareware demo)

It was way harder than the other ports like Quake and DOOM I did because they already had lots of open source projects and work behind them

In case of Battlefield 1942 there was literally absolutely nothing to work on top of, nobody had ever ported it and there was no open source engine for it, nor did the makers ever open source it (like id Software did with Quake 3)

I tried it 6 months ago and essentiay gave up but I tried it today again with Opus 5.5 asking "can you try port the BF1942 demo in this folder to web"

So me and Claude Code (well let's be honest mostly Claude Code) did crazy shit today:
- it disassembled the x86 raw machine code to find 57,000 x86 functions
- it translated each x86 function into a C function (mov eax, [esi+0x110] becomes eax = READ32(esi + 0x110), I have no idea what any of this means btw)
- it outputed 100,000 lines of C
- it then compiled that to WebAsswmbly with Emscripten
- there were 300x Windows and Direct3D functions used which we had to rewrite to WebGL 2 and OpenGL to work on the web
- then we had to build our own network stack so it could connect to our multiplayer server via WebSockets

I have no idea how it did any of this but it did it and it seems to work! 😊 

Come play and report any bugs here!

items.title: Should you rely on public benchmark scores when choosing a model? @VikParuchuri argues "no" in this ...
items.content:
Should you rely on public benchmark scores when choosing a model? @VikParuchuri argues "no" in this talk.

To illustrate this, he shows specific problems found in popular OCR benchmarks:

ParseBench:

• A test expects 310 gigawatts of solar-panel capacity when the correct value is 303.  Additionally, 73% of its chart tests ask for values that aren't printed on the chart. (4:51)

• A test requires "Parish Priest:" to be bold even though those words aren't bold in the source document. (15:33)

• The scorer fails to recognize heading tags placed on separate lines. (16:15)

• dots.mocr ranks last among six models even though it beats the first-ranked model on content and tables.  This is an example of how overall benchmark score can hide important differences in model capabilities. (14:48)

olmOCR-bench:

• A model correctly preserves a line break in a document and gets penalized for it. (10:30)

• A test expects "Republican Party" when a document says "Republican party". Copying the capitalization correctly makes the model fail. (10:49)

• A 700-line postprocessor that rewrites model output adds 1 to 2 points, more than many gaps between models. (12:12)

OmniDocBench:

• This benchmark uses edit distance, which penalizes a correct table written in HTML more heavily than a wrong number in Markdown. So the format matters more than the answer! (6:58)

This is just the tip of the iceberg, the video contains more examples.

Chapters:

0:00 Choosing a model when every vendor claims to be #1
1:54 How OCR benchmark scores improve without better OCR
5:30 Metric design and tests that reject correct answers
11:33 Postprocessing, saturation, and misleading model rankings
12:40 How to slice benchmarks by your task and check for bias
16:53 How to build fair tests with verified answers and consistent scoring
19:05 How to test OCR models on your own documents
24:10 Benchmark marketing, private evals, and how to choose a model

items.content:
I never know what to say when people talk about the “GPU spot market”.

Some clouds have preemptible instances at a discount. These are called “spot” in several clouds. AWS sets a price that goes up and down with demand (very slowly). GCP has monthly prices. Azure has a fixed discount. Some neoclouds like Nebius have auctions.

Some vendors like SpaceX sell short-term non-preemptible capacity at a high price.

There’s no liquid “market” here, at least no marketplace. And there’s confusion about preemptibility.

Feels like the inglorious basterds finger count scene meme a bit.

items.content:
A very tragic crash with a private jet once again

Before this crash the Learjet 60 was had fatal odds per trip of 1 in 1.1 million

To compare a good commercial airline like Delta has a 1 in 25 million odds, many airlines never crashed though so the real odds are even lower like 1 in 40 million trips maybe

So the Learjet 60 was already 40x less safe than commercial airliners

That's something I keep repeating about private jets, they're simply not as safe as flying commercial because:
- pilots require less flight hours
- private aviation is less regulated
- smaller airports with less or no instrument landing systems (ILS)
- smaller planes are more affected by weather (in this case icing)

The Learjet 60 now has fatal odds of 1 in 800,000 which is still about double as safe as the Cessna Citation (one of the most common private jets)

Most Gulfstreams still have flawless safety records though, G500/G600, G550, G650/G700/G800 never crashed, so if you are boarding a private jet anytime soon, I'd say go with them!

Modern LLMs achieve remarkable capabilities, yet the mathematical principles governing how they represent and generate language remain largely unexplained. This lack of theoretical foundation hampers efforts to anticipate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks and misaligned behavior, and limits the ability to design more efficient architectures. The article addresses this challenge by examining whether language models possess an intrinsic, low-dimensional structure that can be captured independently of specific model architectures.

The main objective of the article is to demonstrate that language models exhibit an architecture-agnostic low-rank structure over extended token sequences and to evaluate how this mathematical property can be leveraged for generation and theoretical analysis.

items.title: Tens of millions of taxpayers rely on software to interpret and file federal tax returns every year,...
items.content:
Tens of millions of taxpayers rely on software to interpret and file federal tax returns every year, making tax preparation systems a primary example of legal-critical software. Ensuring compliance is difficult because tax laws are ambiguous, interconnected, and constantly updated. In addition, verifying such systems faces the "oracle problem": software testers rarely have access to a definitive, independent calculation engine to confirm whether an output is legally correct. While LLMs offer strong potential for automating code translation, single LLM implementations frequently hallucinate, misinterpret statutory math (such as applying top tax bracket rates to entire incomes), and perform poorly as statutory complexity increases.

The article aims to design and evaluate an automated multi-agent framework called Synedrion that translates natural language tax regulations into executable code. It specifically evaluates whether a coordinated team of specialized AI agents, combined with advanced automated testing, can match or exceed the accuracy and robustness of single, state-of-the-art models.

items.title: Audio-language models can answer complex questions about sound, but asking them to explain their rea...
items.content:
Audio-language models can answer complex questions about sound, but asking them to explain their reasoning can make them less accurate. As their explanations grow, they may rely on their own generated text instead of the audio, producing answers that sound convincing but are not well grounded. The article investigates whether training can help these models keep the audio evidence in focus without adding cost or delay at use time.

The article introduces SPARE, a fine-tuning method that gives the model an early representation of the intended final conclusion before it generates its reasoning. During training, a special token is encouraged to encode the conclusion’s meaning, using a sentence-embedding model as a target. The team tested the method with SALMONN 13B, training on 160,000 audio examples and evaluating on two benchmarks for audio understanding and reasoning, MMAU and MMAR. They compared it with direct answering, reasoning without fine-tuning, standard fine-tuning, and another method that trains models to predict future text.
